scoreNote: Strong (5): rejects the claim with observation and a clear account of what heroism is, then squarely confronts the strongest counter — media exposure and cynicism — and answers it; coherent and persuasive.

sentences.text: We live in a skeptical age, quick to expose the flaws of anyone we are tempted to admire.
The claim concludes that this skepticism has gone so far that a society can no longer regard any living man or woman as a hero.
I disagree, because heroism rests on great deeds rather than on flawless lives, and people around the world plainly continue to revere the living for exactly such deeds.
First, the claim is contradicted by simple observation.
Ordinary people still risk their lives for strangers, doctors still serve through plagues, and dissidents still defy tyrants, and the public still honors them for it.
Across every country, living figures are admired, thanked, and held up as examples, which would be impossible if heroism had truly become unthinkable.
We have not lost our capacity for admiration; we have only become more careful about where we place it.
The living hero is not extinct; he is simply held to an honest standard.
Walk through any city after a disaster and you will find people calling their rescuers heroes, and meaning it.
A society that still produces courage will always find people to admire.
Moreover, the claim assumes that a hero must be without flaws, and that has never been true.
A hero is someone who does something brave or selfless, not someone who is good in every private respect.
Discovering that a courageous person is also vain, or difficult, or inconsistent does not undo the courage; it merely shows that heroes are human.
Indeed, a flawed person who rises to a great moment is more inspiring than a saint, because his example is one ordinary people can actually follow.
We do not stop honoring those who ran toward danger because we later learn they were imperfect at home.
A statue may need to be spotless; a hero never did.
What our age has abandoned is not heroism but the fantasy that heroes are perfect.
The most compelling case for the claim is that relentless media exposure and public cynicism make it impossible for any reputation to survive intact.
There is real force here, since modern coverage does drag every figure's failings into the light and a knowing cynicism is quick to sneer at anyone praised.
But this confuses the death of the flawless image with the death of heroism, and exposing a hero's faults is not the same as the erasure of his deeds.
Cynics may scoff, yet the firefighter, the rescuer, and the reformer go on being admired by most people precisely because what they did was real.
The cynic's sneer has never once pulled a child from a burning house.
Exposure has changed how we admire our heroes; it has not taken them away.
In conclusion, it remains entirely possible to regard the living as heroes.
Because heroism depends on deeds rather than on spotless lives, the modern exposure of human flaws has retired the false idol, not the real hero.
We can still honor the living; we have only learned to honor people as they are rather than as we once pretended they were.
